newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zaire mineral riches up for grabs as rebels march.
newsitem.headline: Zaire mineral riches up for grabs as rebels march.

text.p: Zaire's abundant mineral wealth in diamonds, base and precious metals is up for grabs as rebel leader Laurent Kabila's soldiers threaten to push into the heart of the country's mining region, analysts said on Tuesday.
The rebels, who took Zaire's third city Kisangani on Saturday, said their next target would be Lubumbashi in Shaba province, 1500 km to the south.
Zaire's vast copper and cobalt wealth is concentrated in Shaba which is also Kabila's home province.
President Mobutu Seso Seko's embattled government is heavily dependent on foreign exchange earned by copper and cobalt from Shaba and diamonds from Kasai province.
Analysts said Zaire is regarded as one of the largest sources of minerals in the world.

"Certainly in the African context, it is regarded as one of the largest, relatively untapped...the geologists would tell you the geological formation and structure of Zaire is conducive to the formation of ore deposits which could yield world-class deposits.

"Obviously the Zambian-Zairean copper belt is a world-class deposit in itself but the rest of Zaire has been relatively unexplored, that is what excites everybody," said RMB Resources director Willo Stear.
Zaire is also the world's fourth-largest diamond producer and the fourth-largest gold producer in Africa.
The country's production of copper and cobalt dropped considerably from highs in the 1980s when the central African country was one of the world's largest producers of the metals.

But recently, state-owned mining giant Gecamines began selling off some its assets to foreign companies and many of the world's major mining houses have submitted bids to develop Gecamines mines up for sale.
Metals analyst Stephen Briggs of stockbroker E.W.Balderson said Gecamines had been given no direction in past years from Kinshasa.
"In recent years the problem has been that Gecamines has been given no direction at all. (President) Mobutu is permanently in hospital and fiddling while Rome burns.

"I think if (Kabila) wins this, he is going to be more hands on and I think he knows that Gecamines is the saviour of Zaire and he would at the very worst encourage joint ventures between Gecamines and foreign companies," Briggs said.
Sources at South African mining companies who tendered for some of Gecamines' projects said they believed Kabila would be welcomed by locals in Shaba and Lubumbashi.
Last week the head of Zaire's state diamond company Societe Miniere de Bakwanga (MIBA), Mukamba Kadiata Nzemba, said he would be ready to collaborate with the rebels.
"If Kabila arrives and he is the new boss, I would obey him. I obeyed Mobutu when he was boss, but he is not immortal," the Financial Times quoted Nzemba as saying.
The Financial Times said Nzemba's announcement that MIBA would work under Kabila's rebels was a significant setback for Mobutu's government.
Briggs said if Kabila took over more of Zaire and especially Shaba province, it would be good news for the country.
"My guess would be in the long term it would be good news. He will resuscitate existing operations and perhaps encourage new ones."
South African mining companies Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd, Gencor Ltd and Iscor Ltd have all tendered to develop the Kolwezi tailings project in Shaba.
Diamond giant De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd maintained about five buying offices in Zaire, a company spokesman said.
